
Expected: Line present: session include       password-auth-ac

**How it works:** RHEL 8.2+ uses pam_faillock configured in /etc/security/faillock.conf (deny, fail_interval, unlock_time, even_deny_root, dir, audit, silent) and wired into system-auth and password-auth by authselect ('authselect enable-feature with-faillock'). Inspect with 'faillock --user <name>' and reset with 'faillock --user <name> --reset'. Pointing 'dir' at a persistent path such as /var/log/faillock keeps lockouts across reboots.

**Operational impact:** Service accounts with stale cached credentials (mapped drives, scheduled tasks, mobile mail clients) can trigger repeated lockouts. Identify the lockout source (Windows Event ID 4740; faillock and audit logs on Linux) before loosening the threshold.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify "system-auth" and "password-auth" files are symbolic links pointing to "system-auth-local" and "password-auth-local":
     $ sudo ls -l /etc/pam.d/{password,system}-auth

     lrwxrwxrwx. 1 root root 30 Apr 1 11:59 /etc/pam.d/password-auth -> /etc/pam.d/password-auth-local
     lrwxrwxrwx. 1 root root 28 Apr 1 11:59 /etc/pam.d/system-auth -> /etc/pam.d/system-auth-local

If system-auth and password-auth files are not symbolic links, this is a finding.

If system-auth and password-auth are symbolic links but do not point to "system-auth-local" and "password-auth-local", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Create custom configuration files and their corresponding symbolic links:

Rename the existing configuration files (skip this step if symbolic links are already present):
     $ sudo mv /etc/pam.d/system-auth /etc/pam.d/system-auth-ac
     $ sudo mv /etc/pam.d/password-auth /etc/pam.d/password-auth-ac

Create custom system-auth configuration file:
     $ sudo vi /etc/pam.d/system-auth-local

The new file, at minimum, must contain the following lines:

auth        required      pam_faillock.so preauth silent audit deny=3 even_deny_root fail_interval=900 unlock_time=900
auth        include       system-auth-ac
auth        sufficient    pam_unix.so try_first_pass
auth        [default=die] pam_faillock.so authfail audit deny=3 even_deny_root fail_interval=900 unlock_time=900

account     required      pam_faillock.so
account     include       system-auth-ac

password    requisite     pam_pwhistory.so remember=5 retry=3
password    requisite     pam_pwquality.so retry=3
password    include       system-auth-ac
password    sufficient    pam_unix.so sha512 shadow try_first_pass use_authtok

session     include       system-auth-ac

Create custom password-auth configuration file:
     $ sudo vi /etc/pam.d/password-auth-local

The new file, at minimum, must contain the following lines:

auth        required      pam_faillock.so preauth silent audit deny=3 even_deny_root fail_interval=900 unlock_time=900
auth        include       password-auth-ac
auth        sufficient    pam_unix.so try_first_pass
auth        [default=die] pam_faillock.so authfail audit deny=3 even_deny_root fail_interval=900 unlock_time=900

account     required      pam_faillock.so
account     include       password-auth-ac

password    requisite     pam_pwhistory.so use_authtok remember=5 retry=3
password    requisite     pam_pwquality.so retry=3
password    include       password-auth-ac
password    sufficient    pam_unix.so sha512 shadow try_first_pass use_authtok

session     include       password-auth-ac

Create new or move existing symbolic links to the new custom configuration files:
     $ sudo ln -sf /etc/pam.d/system-auth-local /etc/pam.d/system-auth
     $ sudo ln -sf /etc/pam.d/password-auth-local /etc/pam.d/password-auth

Once finished, the following file structure should be present:
    $ sudo ls -1 /etc/pam.d/{password,system}-auth*

    /etc/pam.d/password-auth
    /etc/pam.d/password-auth-ac
    /etc/pam.d/password-auth-local
    /etc/pam.d/system-auth
    /etc/pam.d/system-auth-ac
    /etc/pam.d/system-auth-local

Note: With this solution in place, any custom settings to "system-auth" and "password-auth" will be retained and not overwritten by the use of the authconfig utility. The authconfig utility will write its settings to "system-auth-ac" and "password-auth-ac" and continue to function as expected.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** When using the authconfig utility to modify authentication configuration settings, the "system-auth" and "password-auth" files and any custom settings that they may contain are overwritten. This can be avoided by creating new local configuration files and creating new or moving existing symbolic links to them. The authconfig utility will recognize the local configuration files and not overwrite them, while writing its own settings to the original configuration files.

**Threat & control context:** Lockout thresholds turn online password guessing from an unlimited search into a handful of attempts per window (AC-7). The trade-off is denial of service: an attacker who knows usernames can deliberately lock out accounts, which is why DoD pairs a low threshold (3) with an administrator-unlock or timed-unlock requirement. Lockout does nothing against offline cracking of stolen hashes or against password spraying that stays below the threshold, so it complements, rather than replaces, password strength and MFA.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing; T1110.003 Brute Force: Password Spraying

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000196**: The information system, for password-based authentication, stores only cryptographically-protected passwords.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: IA-5 (1) (c) · Rev 3: IA-5 (1) (c)

### V-204415 · RHEL-07-010200 · CAT II: The Red Hat Enterprise Linux operating system must be configured so that the PAM system service is configured to store only encrypted representations of passwords.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-204415r982199_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000073-GPOS-00041 |
| Topic | Credential Storage & Password Hashing, Authentication Stack (PAM, SSSD, Directory) |
| CCI | CCI-000196 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | n/a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-5 (1) (c) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-5 (1) (c) |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured so that the PAM system service is configured to store only encrypted representations of passwords.

**Why it matters:** Computers shouldn't store your actual password. Instead they store a scrambled "fingerprint" of it that can't be turned back into the password. This rule makes sure that fingerprint is created with a strong method, so that even if someone steals the file, they can't easily work out everyone's passwords.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *PAM*: Pluggable Authentication Modules: the Linux component that checks passwords and other sign-in requirements.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/pam.d/system-auth | password | sufficient    pam_unix.so sha512 shadow try_first_pass use_authtok |
| Config | /etc/pam.d/password-auth | password | sufficient    pam_unix.so sha512 shadow try_first_pass use_authtok |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep password /etc/pam.d/system-auth /etc/pam.d/password-auth
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
grep -rs 'pam_unix.so' /etc/pam.d/system-auth
```

Expected: Line present: password sufficient    pam_unix.so sha512 shadow try_first_pass use_authtok

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
grep -rs 'pam_unix.so' /etc/pam.d/password-auth
```

Expected: Line present: password sufficient    pam_unix.so sha512 shadow try_first_pass use_authtok

**How it works:** On RHEL, hashes are stored in /etc/shadow. The algorithm for new passwords comes from ENCRYPT_METHOD (and SHA_CRYPT_MIN_ROUNDS) in /etc/login.defs, 'crypt_style' in /etc/libuser.conf, and the pam_unix module options. Existing hashes are upgraded only when users change their passwords. Check the hash prefix in /etc/shadow ($6$ = SHA-512).

**Also related (Authentication Stack (PAM, SSSD, Directory)):** On RHEL, PAM stacks live in /etc/pam.d/ (system-auth, password-auth, login, sshd, su). Manage them through authselect profiles ('authselect select sssd with-faillock with-mkhomedir ...', 'authselect current'), because authselect overwrites hand edits. Custom changes belong in a custom profile ('authselect create-profile'). SSSD is configured in /etc/sssd/sssd.conf and conf.d/ (mode 0600, owned by root), and you restart sssd after changes. Concurrent session limits are set in /etc/security/limits.conf ('* hard maxlogins 10').

**Operational impact:** Reducing cached logons can prevent laptop users from signing in when they are off the network. Disabling LM hashes affects only very old clients (pre-Windows 2000 era).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the PAM system service is configured to store only encrypted representations of passwords. The strength of encryption that must be used to hash passwords for all accounts is SHA512.

Check that the system is configured to create SHA512 hashed passwords with the following command:

     # grep password /etc/pam.d/system-auth /etc/pam.d/password-auth

Outcome should look like following:
     /etc/pam.d/system-auth-ac:password    sufficient    pam_unix.so sha512 shadow try_first_pass use_authtok
     /etc/pam.d/password-auth:password     sufficient    pam_unix.so sha512 shadow try_first_pass use_authtok

If the "/etc/pam.d/system-auth" and "/etc/pam.d/password-auth" configuration files allow for password hashes other than SHA512 to be used, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the operating system to store only SHA512 encrypted representations of passwords.

Add the following line in "/etc/pam.d/system-auth":
     password    sufficient    pam_unix.so sha512 shadow try_first_pass use_authtok

Add the following line in "/etc/pam.d/password-auth":
     password    sufficient    pam_unix.so sha512 shadow try_first_pass use_authtok

Note: Per requirement RHEL-07-010199, RHEL 7 must be configured to not overwrite custom authentication configuration settings while using the authconfig utility; otherwise, manual changes to the listed files will be overwritten whenever the authconfig utility is used.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Passwords need to be protected at all times, and encryption is the standard method for protecting passwords. If passwords are not encrypted, they can be plainly read (i.e., clear text) and easily compromised. Passwords encrypted with a weak algorithm are no more protected than if they are kept in plain text.

**Threat & control context:** When a host is compromised, stored credential material is the attacker's path to lateral movement. Weak or reversible storage (LM hashes, reversible encryption, low-iteration hashes, excessive cached domain logons) turns a single compromise into credential recovery for many accounts. IA-5(1)(c) requires that only cryptographically protected passwords be stored and transmitted. Strong salted, iterated hashing such as SHA-512 crypt with sufficient rounds increases offline cracking cost.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1110.002 Brute Force: Password Cracking; T1552 Unsecured Credentials; T1556.003 Modify Authentication Process: Pluggable Authentication Modules; T1110 Brute Force

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000196**: The information system, for password-based authentication, stores only cryptographically-protected passwords.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: IA-5 (1) (c) · Rev 3: IA-5 (1) (c)

**Legacy IDs:** V-71919, SV-86543

### V-204416 · RHEL-07-010210 · CAT II: The Red Hat Enterprise Linux operating system must be configured to use the shadow file to store only encrypted representations of passwords.

| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured to use the shadow file to store only encrypted representations of passwords.

**Why it matters:** Computers shouldn't store your actual password. Instead they store a scrambled "fingerprint" of it that can't be turned back into the password. This rule makes sure that fingerprint is created with a strong method, so that even if someone steals the file, they can't easily work out everyone's passwords.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/login.defs | ENCRYPT_METHOD | SHA512 |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep -i encrypt /etc/login.defs
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo grep -si '^[[:space:]]*ENCRYPT_METHOD\b' /etc/login.defs
```

Expected: ENCRYPT_METHOD = SHA512

**How it works:** On RHEL, hashes are stored in /etc/shadow. The algorithm for new passwords comes from ENCRYPT_METHOD (and SHA_CRYPT_MIN_ROUNDS) in /etc/login.defs, 'crypt_style' in /etc/libuser.conf, and the pam_unix module options. Existing hashes are upgraded only when users change their passwords. Check the hash prefix in /etc/shadow ($6$ = SHA-512).

**Operational impact:** Reducing cached logons can prevent laptop users from signing in when they are off the network. Disabling LM hashes affects only very old clients (pre-Windows 2000 era).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the system's shadow file is configured to store only encrypted representations of passwords. The strength of encryption that must be used to hash passwords for all accounts is SHA512.

Check that the system is configured to create SHA512 hashed passwords with the following command:

# grep -i encrypt /etc/login.defs
ENCRYPT_METHOD SHA512

If the "/etc/login.defs" configuration file does not exist or allows for password hashes other than SHA512 to be used, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the operating system to store only SHA512 encrypted representations of passwords.

Add or update the following line in "/etc/login.defs":

ENCRYPT_METHOD SHA512
```

IA-5(1)(c) requires that only cryptographically protected passwords be stored and transmitted. Strong salted, iterated hashing such as SHA-512 crypt with sufficient rounds increases offline cracking cost.

### V-204418 · RHEL-07-010230 · CAT II: The Red Hat Enterprise Linux operating system must be configured so that passwords for new users are restricted to a 24 hours/1 day minimum lifetime.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-204418r982188_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000075-GPOS-00043 |
| Topic | Password Age, History & Reuse |
| CCI | CCI-000198 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | n/a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-5 (1) (d) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-5 (1) (d) |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured so that passwords for new users are restricted to a 24 hours/1 day minimum lifetime.

**Why it matters:** This makes people change passwords every so often and stops them from simply switching back to a password they used recently. If a password was quietly stolen, it eventually stops working, a bit like changing the locks periodically in case someone copied a key.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/login.defs | PASS_MIN_DAYS | 1 |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep -i pass_min_days /etc/login.defs
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo grep -si '^[[:space:]]*PASS_MIN_DAYS\b' /etc/login.defs
```

Expected: PASS_MIN_DAYS = 1

**How it works:** On RHEL, defaults for new accounts come from /etc/login.defs (PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS), while existing accounts must be updated individually with 'chage -M/-m <days> <user>' (review with 'chage -l <user>'). History is enforced by pam_pwhistory ('remember = 5' in /etc/security/pwhistory.conf or on the module line).

**Operational impact:** Changing login.defs does not retroactively update existing accounts, so remember to run chage for current users. Exclude non-interactive service accounts from expiry only through a documented exception (or use gMSAs on Windows).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the operating system enforces 24 hours/1 day as the minimum password lifetime for new user accounts.

Check for the value of "PASS_MIN_DAYS" in "/etc/login.defs" with the following command:

# grep -i pass_min_days /etc/login.defs
PASS_MIN_DAYS     1

If the "PASS_MIN_DAYS" parameter value is not "1" or greater, or is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the operating system to enforce 24 hours/1 day as the minimum password lifetime.

Add the following line in "/etc/login.defs" (or modify the line to have the required value):

PASS_MIN_DAYS     1
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Enforcing a minimum password lifetime helps to prevent repeated password changes to defeat the password reuse or history enforcement requirement. If users are allowed to immediately and continually change their password, the password could be repeatedly changed in a short period of time to defeat the organization's policy regarding password reuse.

**Threat & control context:** Maximum age bounds the useful lifetime of a compromised credential. Minimum age plus history prevent users from cycling straight back to a known password, which would defeat the history check (IA-5(1)(d)/(e)). The trend in current guidance is to prefer event-driven rotation (on suspected compromise) over periodic rotation, but the DoD baseline values remain enforceable requirements.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110.004 Brute Force: Credential Stuffing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000198**: The information system enforces minimum password lifetime restrictions.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: IA-5 (1) (d) · Rev 3: IA-5 (1) (d)

**Legacy IDs:** V-71925, SV-86549

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/pam.d/system-auth | password | requisite     pam_pwhistory.so remember=5 retry=3 |
| Config | /etc/pam.d/password-auth | password | requisite     pam_pwhistory.so use_authtok remember=5 retry=3 |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep -i remember /etc/pam.d/system-auth /etc/pam.d/password-auth
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
grep -rs 'pam_pwhistory.so' /etc/pam.d/system-auth
```

Expected: Line present: password requisite     pam_pwhistory.so remember=5 retry=3

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
grep -rs 'pam_pwhistory.so' /etc/pam.d/password-auth
```

Expected: Line present: password requisite     pam_pwhistory.so use_authtok remember=5 retry=3

**How it works:** On RHEL, defaults for new accounts come from /etc/login.defs (PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS), while existing accounts must be updated individually with 'chage -M/-m <days> <user>' (review with 'chage -l <user>'). History is enforced by pam_pwhistory ('remember = 5' in /etc/security/pwhistory.conf or on the module line).

**Operational impact:** Changing login.defs does not retroactively update existing accounts, so remember to run chage for current users. Exclude non-interactive service accounts from expiry only through a documented exception (or use gMSAs on Windows).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the operating system prohibits password reuse for a minimum of five generations.

Check for the value of the "remember" argument in "/etc/pam.d/system-auth" and "/etc/pam.d/password-auth" with the following command:

     # grep -i remember /etc/pam.d/system-auth /etc/pam.d/password-auth
     password     requisite     pam_pwhistory.so use_authtok remember=5 retry=3

If the line containing the "pam_pwhistory.so" line does not have the "remember" module argument set, is commented out, or the value of the "remember" module argument is set to less than "5", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the operating system to prohibit password reuse for a minimum of five generations.

Add the following line in "/etc/pam.d/system-auth" (or modify the line to have the required value):

password     requisite     pam_pwhistory.so remember=5 retry=3

Add the following line in "/etc/pam.d/password-auth" (or modify the line to have the required value):

password     requisite     pam_pwhistory.so use_authtok remember=5 retry=3

Note: Per requirement RHEL-07-010199, RHEL 7 must be configured to not overwrite custom authentication configuration settings while using the authconfig utility; otherwise, manual changes to the listed files will be overwritten whenever the authconfig utility is used.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Password complexity, or strength, is a measure of the effectiveness of a password in resisting attempts at guessing and brute-force attacks. If the information system or application allows the user to consecutively reuse their password when that password has exceeded its defined lifetime, the end result is a password that is not changed per policy requirements.

**Threat & control context:** Maximum age bounds the useful lifetime of a compromised credential. Minimum age plus history prevent users from cycling straight back to a known password, which would defeat the history check (IA-5(1)(d)/(e)). The trend in current guidance is to prefer event-driven rotation (on suspected compromise) over periodic rotation, but the DoD baseline values remain enforceable requirements.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110.004 Brute Force: Credential Stuffing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000200**: The information system prohibits password reuse for the organization-defined number of generations.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: IA-5 (1) (e) · Rev 3: IA-5 (1) (e)

**Legacy IDs:** V-71933, SV-86557

### V-254523 · RHEL-07-010271 · CAT II: The Red Hat Enterprise Linux operating system must automatically expire temporary accounts within 72 hours.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254523r958508_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000123-GPOS-00064 |
| Topic | Account Lifecycle Management |
| CCI | CCI-001682 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-2 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-2 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-2 (2) |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must automatically expire temporary accounts within 72 hours.

**Why it matters:** Every person should have their own account, and accounts that nobody is using (people who left, temporary contractors, test accounts) should be turned off. Forgotten accounts are like old keys still floating around after someone moves out. You never know who might use them.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
chage -l <temporary_account_name> | grep -i "account expires"
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** On RHEL, inactivity is enforced with 'INACTIVE=35' in /etc/default/useradd ('useradd -D -f 35') for new accounts and 'chage -I' for existing ones. Temporary accounts get an expiry date ('chage -E'). Check /etc/passwd and /etc/group for duplicate UIDs and GIDs ('pwck', 'grpck') and that every interactive user has a valid, owned home directory.

**Operational impact:** Before you automatically disable inactive accounts, confirm that service, break-glass and seasonal-user accounts are inventoried and either exempted with documentation or monitored.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify temporary accounts have been provisioned with an expiration date of 72 hours.

For every existing temporary account, run the following command to obtain its account expiration information:

     $ sudo chage -l <temporary_account_name> | grep -i "account expires"

Verify each of these accounts has an expiration date set within 72 hours.
If any temporary accounts have no expiration date set or do not expire within 72 hours, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the operating system to expire temporary accounts after 72 hours with the following command:

     $ sudo chage -E $(date -d +3days +%Y-%m-%d) <temporary_account_name>
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Temporary accounts are privileged or nonprivileged accounts that are established during pressing circumstances, such as new software or hardware configuration or an incident response, where the need for prompt account activation requires bypassing normal account authorization procedures. If any inactive temporary accounts are left enabled on the system and are not either manually removed or automatically expired within 72 hours, the security posture of the system will be degraded and exposed to exploitation by unauthorized users or insider threat actors.

Temporary accounts are different from emergency accounts. Emergency accounts, also known as "last resort" or "break glass" accounts, are local logon accounts enabled on the system for emergency use by authorized system administrators to manage a system when standard logon methods are failing or not available. Emergency accounts are not subject to manual removal or scheduled expiration requirements.

The automatic expiration of temporary accounts may be extended as needed by the circumstances but it must not be extended indefinitely. A documented permanent account should be established for privileged users who need long-term maintenance accounts.

**Threat & control context:** Dormant, orphaned and shared accounts are prime persistence and initial-access vectors because nobody notices their use. AC-2 (Account Management) and its enhancements (AC-2(2) temporary/emergency account removal, AC-2(3) disable inactive accounts) require automated lifecycle enforcement. IA-2 and IA-4 require unique identifiers so actions can be attributed to individuals. Assessors typically sample accounts against an authoritative roster.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1136 Create Account; T1098 Account Manipulation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001682**: Automatically remove or disable emergency accounts after an organization-defined time period for each type of account.  
  Rev 5: AC-2 (2) · Rev 4: AC-2 (2) · Rev 3: AC-2 (2)

### V-204423 · RHEL-07-010280 · CAT II: The Red Hat Enterprise Linux operating system must be configured so that passwords are a minimum of 15 characters in length.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-204423r982202_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000078-GPOS-00046 |
| Topic | Password Strength & Complexity |
| CCI | CCI-000205 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | n/a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-5 (1) (a) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-5 (1) (a) |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured so that passwords are a minimum of 15 characters in length.

**Why it matters:** This sets the rules for how strong a password must be: long enough, and mixing capitals, lowercase letters, numbers and symbols. Short or simple passwords can be guessed by computers in seconds. A long, varied password is like a key with many unique notches that's much harder to copy.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/security/pwquality.conf | minlen | 15 |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sudo grep minlen /etc/security/pwquality.conf
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo grep -si '^[[:space:]]*minlen\b' /etc/security/pwquality.conf
```

Expected: minlen = 15

**How it works:** RHEL enforces this through pam_pwquality, configured in /etc/security/pwquality.conf or a drop-in under /etc/security/pwquality.conf.d/ (minlen, dcredit/ucredit/lcredit/ocredit as negative numbers meaning 'at least N', minclass, maxrepeat, maxclassrepeat, difok, dictcheck). The pam_pwquality module must appear in the password stack of system-auth and password-auth. Test with 'pwscore' or by changing a test user's password.

**Operational impact:** Takes effect at each user's next password change. Communicate the new requirements beforehand, and check that provisioning scripts and self-service reset portals can generate compliant passwords.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the operating system enforces a minimum 15-character password length. The "minlen" option sets the minimum number of characters in a new password.

Check for the value of the "minlen" option in "/etc/security/pwquality.conf" with the following command:

# grep minlen /etc/security/pwquality.conf
minlen = 15

If the command does not return a "minlen" value of 15 or greater, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure operating system to enforce a minimum 15-character password length.

Add the following line to "/etc/security/pwquality.conf" (or modify the line to have the required value):

minlen = 15
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The shorter the password, the lower the number of possible combinations that need to be tested before the password is compromised.

Password complexity, or strength, is a measure of the effectiveness of a password in resisting attempts at guessing and brute-force attacks. Password length is one factor of several that helps to determine strength and how long it takes to crack a password. Use of more characters in a password helps to exponentially increase the time and/or resources required to compromise the password.

**Threat & control context:** Length and composition rules raise the cost of both online guessing and offline cracking of captured hashes (IA-5(1)). DoD still requires a 15-character minimum with character-class rules, while NIST SP 800-63B now favors length plus breached-password screening over composition rules. Where the two conflict, the STIG governs for DoD systems. Note that complexity rules apply only when a password is changed, so assess the age of existing passwords too.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1110.002 Brute Force: Password Cracking; T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000205**: The information system enforces minimum password length.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: IA-5 (1) (a) · Rev 3: IA-5 (1) (a)

**Legacy IDs:** V-71935, SV-86559

### V-204424 · RHEL-07-010290 · CAT I: The Red Hat Enterprise Linux operating system must not allow accounts configured with blank or null passwords.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-204424r991589_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Built-in & Privileged Account Hardening |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must not allow accounts configured with blank or null passwords.

**Why it matters:** Every computer comes with a few built-in "master" accounts whose names everyone knows. This rule makes those accounts harder to abuse, for example by not letting anyone log in directly as the master account and never allowing accounts with no password. It's like not leaving the master key labelled "MASTER KEY" hanging by the front door.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep nullok /etc/pam.d/system-auth /etc/pam.d/password-auth
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** On RHEL, root logon is controlled through sshd ('PermitRootLogin no'), /etc/securetty (where present), and PAM. Empty passwords are blocked by removing 'nullok' from pam_unix in system-auth and password-auth and by setting 'PermitEmptyPasswords no' for sshd. Only root should have UID 0 ('awk -F: "$3==0" /etc/passwd').

**Operational impact:** Make sure at least one named administrator account with sudo or admin rights works before disabling root or Administrator logon paths. Renaming the built-in Administrator can break scripts that reference it by name.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
To verify that null passwords cannot be used, run the following command:

     # grep nullok /etc/pam.d/system-auth /etc/pam.d/password-auth

If this produces any output, it may be possible to log on with accounts with empty passwords.

If null passwords can be used, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
If an account is configured for password authentication but does not have an assigned password, it may be possible to log on to the account without authenticating.

Remove any instances of the "nullok" option in "/etc/pam.d/system-auth" and "/etc/pam.d/password-auth" to prevent logons with empty passwords.

Note: Per requirement RHEL-07-010199, RHEL 7 must be configured to not overwrite custom authentication configuration settings while using the authconfig utility, otherwise manual changes to the listed files will be overwritten whenever the authconfig utility is used.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** If an account has an empty password, anyone could log on and run commands with the privileges of that account. Accounts with empty passwords should never be used in operational environments.

**Threat & control context:** Well-known accounts (root, Administrator, Guest) are guaranteed to exist with predictable names, which makes them ideal targets. Blocking direct logon forces attribution through named accounts (IA-2, AC-6(2)). Removing empty-password acceptance eliminates trivial access, and unique local admin passwords (LAPS) break pass-the-hash lateral movement across a fleet. Assess the effective result across every access path: console, SSH, RDP and network logon.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078.001 Valid Accounts: Default Accounts; T1078.003 Valid Accounts: Local Accounts; T1110 Brute Force

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

**Legacy IDs:** V-71937, SV-86561

### V-204425 · RHEL-07-010300 · CAT I: The Red Hat Enterprise Linux operating system must be configured so that the SSH daemon does not allow authentication using an empty password.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-204425r958486_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000106-GPOS-00053 |
| Topic | SSH Remote Administration, Built-in & Privileged Account Hardening |
| CCI | CCI-000766 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-2 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-2 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-2 (2) |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured so that the SSH daemon does not allow authentication using an empty password.

**Why it matters:** SSH is the secure "remote control" administrators use to manage the computer over the network by typing commands. This rule tightens how that remote control works: who may use it, how they prove their identity, and how idle connections are closed. It's like making sure the building's service entrance has a good lock and isn't propped open.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

**Key terms:**
- *SSH*: Secure Shell: an encrypted way to control a computer remotely by typing commands.
- *PAM*: Pluggable Authentication Modules: the Linux component that checks passwords and other sign-in requirements.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/ssh/sshd_config | PermitEmptyPasswords | no |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sudo grep -i PermitEmptyPasswords /etc/ssh/sshd_config
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo sshd -T | grep -i '^PermitEmptyPasswords '
```

Expected: permitemptypasswords no (the effective value sshd is using).

**How it works:** sshd reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config, and on RHEL 9/10 also drop-ins under /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ that are processed in lexical order, where the first value obtained wins. Put STIG settings in an early-sorting drop-in (e.g. 00-stig.conf) so a vendor file can't silently override them. Validate syntax with 'sshd -t', check the effective configuration with 'sshd -T | grep -i <keyword>', then 'systemctl reload sshd'.

**Also related (Built-in & Privileged Account Hardening):** On RHEL, root logon is controlled through sshd ('PermitRootLogin no'), /etc/securetty (where present), and PAM. Empty passwords are blocked by removing 'nullok' from pam_unix in system-auth and password-auth and by setting 'PermitEmptyPasswords no' for sshd. Only root should have UID 0 ('awk -F: "$3==0" /etc/passwd').

**Operational impact:** Keep an existing session open while you reload sshd so a typo can't lock you out. Disabling root login requires named admin accounts plus sudo. Idle timeouts (ClientAliveInterval/CountMax) will disconnect long-running interactive sessions, so use tmux or screen for those.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
To determine how the SSH daemon's "PermitEmptyPasswords" option is set, run the following command:

# grep -i PermitEmptyPasswords /etc/ssh/sshd_config
PermitEmptyPasswords no

If no line, a commented line, or a line indicating the value "no" is returned, the required value is set.

If the required value is not set, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
To explicitly disallow remote logon from accounts with empty passwords, add or correct the following line in "/etc/ssh/sshd_config":

PermitEmptyPasswords no

The SSH service must be restarted for changes to take effect.  Any accounts with empty passwords should be disabled immediately, and PAM configuration should prevent users from being able to assign themselves empty passwords.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Configuring this setting for the SSH daemon provides additional assurance that remote logon via SSH will require a password, even in the event of misconfiguration elsewhere.

**Threat & control context:** SSH is the primary remote administration channel on Linux and therefore a high-value target. Hardening reduces the attack surface: no root or empty-password logins, no host-based trust (rhosts) or user environment injection, strict file-mode checks, idle-session termination, and approved cryptography only. These settings support AC-17 (Remote Access), AC-12, IA-2 and SC-8. Also check authorized_keys sprawl and key lifecycle, which no STIG setting fully covers.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1021.004 Remote Services: SSH; T1110 Brute Force; T1098.004 Account Manipulation: SSH Authorized Keys; T1078.001 Valid Accounts: Default Accounts; T1078.003 Valid Accounts: Local Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000766**: Implement multifactor authentication for access to non-privileged accounts.  
  Rev 5: IA-2 (2) · Rev 4: IA-2 (2) · Rev 3: IA-2 (2)

**Legacy IDs:** SV-86563, V-71939

### V-204426 · RHEL-07-010310 · CAT II: The Red Hat Enterprise Linux operating system must disable account identifiers (individuals, groups, roles, and devices) if the password expires.

**In plain terms:** This computer must disable account identifiers (individuals, groups, roles, and devices) if the password expires.

**Why it matters:** This makes people change passwords every so often and stops them from simply switching back to a password they used recently. If a password was quietly stolen, it eventually stops working, a bit like changing the locks periodically in case someone copied a key.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/default/useradd | INACTIVE | 35 |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep -i inactive /etc/default/useradd
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo grep -rsi '^[[:space:]]*INACTIVE\b' /etc/default/useradd
```

Expected: INACTIVE = 35

**How it works:** On RHEL, defaults for new accounts come from /etc/login.defs (PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS), while existing accounts must be updated individually with 'chage -M/-m <days> <user>' (review with 'chage -l <user>'). History is enforced by pam_pwhistory ('remember = 5' in /etc/security/pwhistory.conf or on the module line).

**Also related (Account Lifecycle Management):** On RHEL, inactivity is enforced with 'INACTIVE=35' in /etc/default/useradd ('useradd -D -f 35') for new accounts and 'chage -I' for existing ones. Temporary accounts get an expiry date ('chage -E'). Check /etc/passwd and /etc/group for duplicate UIDs and GIDs ('pwck', 'grpck') and that every interactive user has a valid, owned home directory.

**Operational impact:** Changing login.defs does not retroactively update existing accounts, so remember to run chage for current users. Exclude non-interactive service accounts from expiry only through a documented exception (or use gMSAs on Windows).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If passwords are not being used for authentication, this is Not Applicable.

Verify the operating system disables account identifiers (individuals, groups, roles, and devices) after the password has expired with the following command:

     # grep -i inactive /etc/default/useradd
     INACTIVE=35

If "INACTIVE" is set to "-1", a value greater than "35", is commented out, or is not defined, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the operating system to disable account identifiers (individuals, groups, roles, and devices) 35 days after the password has expired.

Add the following line to "/etc/default/useradd" (or modify the line to have the required value):

     INACTIVE=35

DOD recommendation is 35 days, but a lower value is acceptable. The value "-1" will disable this feature, and "0" will disable the account immediately after the password expires.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Inactive identifiers pose a risk to systems and applications because attackers may exploit an inactive identifier and potentially obtain undetected access to the system. Owners of inactive accounts will not notice if unauthorized access to their user account has been obtained.

Operating systems need to track periods of inactivity and disable application identifiers after 35 days of inactivity.

**Threat & control context:** Maximum age bounds the useful lifetime of a compromised credential. Minimum age plus history prevent users from cycling straight back to a known password, which would defeat the history check (IA-5(1)(d)/(e)). The trend in current guidance is to prefer event-driven rotation (on suspected compromise) over periodic rotation, but the DoD baseline values remain enforceable requirements.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110.004 Brute Force: Credential Stuffing; T1136 Create Account; T1098 Account Manipulation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000795**: The organization manages information system identifiers by disabling the identifier after an organization-defined time period of inactivity.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: IA-4 e · Rev 3: IA-4 e

**Legacy IDs:** SV-86565, V-71941

### V-204427 · RHEL-07-010320 · CAT II: The Red Hat Enterprise Linux operating system must be configured to lock accounts for a minimum of 15 minutes after three unsuccessful logon attempts within a 15-minute timeframe.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-204427r958736_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000329-GPOS-00128 |
| Topic | Account Lockout |
| CCI | CCI-000044, CCI-002236, CCI-002237, CCI-002238 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-7 a, AC-7 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-7 a, AC-7 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-7 a |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured to lock accounts for a minimum of 15 minutes after three unsuccessful logon attempts within a 15-minute timeframe.

**Why it matters:** If someone types the wrong password a few times in a row, the account is temporarily locked so they can't keep guessing. It's like a phone that freezes after several wrong passcodes, which stops a thief from trying every possible combination.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *PAM*: Pluggable Authentication Modules: the Linux component that checks passwords and other sign-in requirements.
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/pam.d/password-auth | auth | sufficient    pam_unix.so try_first_pass |
| Config | /etc/pam.d/password-auth | account | required      pam_faillock.so |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep pam_faillock.so /etc/pam.d/password-auth
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep pam_faillock.so /etc/pam.d/system-auth
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
grep -rs 'pam_unix.so' /etc/pam.d/password-auth
```

Expected: Line present: auth sufficient    pam_unix.so try_first_pass

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
grep -rs 'pam_faillock.so' /etc/pam.d/password-auth
```

Expected: Line present: account required      pam_faillock.so

**How it works:** RHEL 8.2+ uses pam_faillock configured in /etc/security/faillock.conf (deny, fail_interval, unlock_time, even_deny_root, dir, audit, silent) and wired into system-auth and password-auth by authselect ('authselect enable-feature with-faillock'). Inspect with 'faillock --user <name>' and reset with 'faillock --user <name> --reset'. Pointing 'dir' at a persistent path such as /var/log/faillock keeps lockouts across reboots.

**Operational impact:** Service accounts with stale cached credentials (mapped drives, scheduled tasks, mobile mail clients) can trigger repeated lockouts. Identify the lockout source (Windows Event ID 4740; faillock and audit logs on Linux) before loosening the threshold.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Check that the system locks an account for a minimum of 15 minutes after three unsuccessful logon attempts within a period of 15 minutes with the following command:

     # grep pam_faillock.so /etc/pam.d/password-auth

auth        required      pam_faillock.so preauth silent audit deny=3 even_deny_root fail_interval=900 unlock_time=900
auth        [default=die] pam_faillock.so authfail audit deny=3 even_deny_root fail_interval=900 unlock_time=900
account     required      pam_faillock.so

If the "deny" parameter is set to "0" or a value greater than "3" on both "auth" lines with the "pam_faillock.so" module, or is missing from these lines, this is a finding.

If the "even_deny_root" parameter is not set on both "auth" lines with the "pam_faillock.so" module, or is missing from these lines, this is a finding.

If the "fail_interval" parameter is set to "0" or is set to a value less than "900" on both "auth" lines with the "pam_faillock.so" module, or is missing from these lines, this is a finding.

If the "unlock_time" parameter is not set to "0", "never", or is set to a value less than "900" on both "auth" lines with the "pam_faillock.so" module, or is missing from these lines, this is a finding.

Note: The maximum configurable value for "unlock_time" is "604800".

If any line referencing the "pam_faillock.so" module is commented out, this is a finding.

     # grep pam_faillock.so /etc/pam.d/system-auth

auth        required      pam_faillock.so preauth silent audit deny=3 even_deny_root fail_interval=900 unlock_time=900
auth        [default=die] pam_faillock.so authfail audit deny=3 even_deny_root fail_interval=900 unlock_time=900
account     required      pam_faillock.so

If the "deny" parameter is set to "0" or a value greater than "3" on both "auth" lines with the "pam_faillock.so" module, or is missing from these lines, this is a finding.

If the "even_deny_root" parameter is not set on both "auth" lines with the "pam_faillock.so" module, or is missing from these lines, this is a finding.

If the "fail_interval" parameter is set to "0" or is set to a value less than "900" on both "auth" lines with the "pam_faillock.so" module, or is missing from these lines, this is a finding.

If the "unlock_time" parameter is not set to "0", "never", or is set to a value less than "900" on both "auth" lines with the "pam_faillock.so" module or is missing from these lines, this is a finding.

Note: The maximum configurable value for "unlock_time" is "604800".

If any line referencing the "pam_faillock.so" module is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the operating system to lock an account for the maximum period when three unsuccessful logon attempts in 15 minutes are made.

Add/Modify the appropriate sections of the "/etc/pam.d/system-auth" and "/etc/pam.d/password-auth" files to match the following lines:

auth        required      pam_faillock.so preauth silent audit deny=3 even_deny_root fail_interval=900 unlock_time=900
auth        sufficient    pam_unix.so try_first_pass
auth        [default=die] pam_faillock.so authfail audit deny=3 even_deny_root fail_interval=900 unlock_time=900
account     required      pam_faillock.so

Note: Per requirement RHEL-07-010199, RHEL 7 must be configured to not overwrite custom authentication configuration settings while using the authconfig utility, otherwise manual changes to the listed files will be overwritten whenever the authconfig utility is used.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** By limiting the number of failed logon attempts, the risk of unauthorized system access via user password guessing, otherwise known as brute-forcing, is reduced. Limits are imposed by locking the account.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000329-GPOS-00128, SRG-OS-000021-GPOS-00005

**Threat & control context:** Lockout thresholds turn online password guessing from an unlimited search into a handful of attempts per window (AC-7). The trade-off is denial of service: an attacker who knows usernames can deliberately lock out accounts, which is why DoD pairs a low threshold (3) with an administrator-unlock or timed-unlock requirement. Lockout does nothing against offline cracking of stolen hashes or against password spraying that stays below the threshold, so it complements, rather than replaces, password strength and MFA.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing; T1110.003 Brute Force: Password Spraying

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000044**: Enforce the organization-defined limit of consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during the organization-defined time period.  
  Rev 5: AC-7 a · Rev 4: AC-7 a · Rev 3: AC-7 a
- **CCI-002236**: Defines the time period the information system will automatically lock the account or node when the maximum number of unsuccessful logon attempts is exceeded.  
  Rev 5: AC-7 b · Rev 4: AC-7 b · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-002237**: Defines the delay algorithm to delay the next logon prompt when the maximum number of unsuccessful logon attempts is exceeded.  
  Rev 5: AC-7 b · Rev 4: AC-7 b · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-002238**: Automatically lock the account or node for either an organization-defined time period, until the locked account or node is released by an administrator, or delays the next logon prompt according to the organization-defined delay algorithm when the maximum number of unsuccessful logon attempts is exceeded.  
  Rev 5: AC-7 b · Rev 4: AC-7 b · Rev 3: n/a

**Legacy IDs:** V-71943, SV-86567

### V-204428 · RHEL-07-010330 · CAT II: The Red Hat Enterprise Linux operating system must lock the associated account after three unsuccessful root logon attempts are made within a 15-minute period.

| Field | Value |

| Rule ID | `SV-204428r958736_rule` |

| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-7 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-7 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must lock the associated account after three unsuccessful root logon attempts are made within a 15-minute period.

**Why it matters:** Every computer comes with a few built-in "master" accounts whose names everyone knows. This rule makes those accounts harder to abuse, for example by not letting anyone log in directly as the master account and never allowing accounts with no password. It's like not leaving the master key labelled "MASTER KEY" hanging by the front door.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *PAM*: Pluggable Authentication Modules: the Linux component that checks passwords and other sign-in requirements.
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.
- *root*: The all-powerful administrator account on Linux.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/pam.d/password-auth | auth | sufficient    pam_unix.so try_first_pass |
| Config | /etc/pam.d/password-auth | account | required      pam_faillock.so |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep pam_faillock.so /etc/pam.d/password-auth
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep pam_faillock.so /etc/pam.d/system-auth
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
grep -rs 'pam_unix.so' /etc/pam.d/password-auth
```

Expected: Line present: auth sufficient    pam_unix.so try_first_pass

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
grep -rs 'pam_faillock.so' /etc/pam.d/password-auth
```

Expected: Line present: account required      pam_faillock.so

**How it works:** On RHEL, root logon is controlled through sshd ('PermitRootLogin no'), /etc/securetty (where present), and PAM. Empty passwords are blocked by removing 'nullok' from pam_unix in system-auth and password-auth and by setting 'PermitEmptyPasswords no' for sshd. Only root should have UID 0 ('awk -F: "$3==0" /etc/passwd').

**Operational impact:** Make sure at least one named administrator account with sudo or admin rights works before disabling root or Administrator logon paths. Renaming the built-in Administrator can break scripts that reference it by name.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the operating system automatically locks the root account, for a minimum of 15 minutes, when three unsuccessful logon attempts in 15 minutes are made.

     # grep pam_faillock.so /etc/pam.d/password-auth

auth        required      pam_faillock.so preauth silent audit deny=3 even_deny_root fail_interval=900 unlock_time=900
auth        [default=die] pam_faillock.so authfail audit deny=3 even_deny_root fail_interval=900 unlock_time=900
account     required      pam_faillock.so

If the "even_deny_root" setting is not defined on both lines with the "pam_faillock.so" module, is commented out, or is missing from a line, this is a finding.

     # grep pam_faillock.so /etc/pam.d/system-auth

auth        required      pam_faillock.so preauth silent audit deny=3 even_deny_root fail_interval=900 unlock_time=900
auth        [default=die] pam_faillock.so authfail audit deny=3 even_deny_root fail_interval=900 unlock_time=900
account     required      pam_faillock.so

If the "even_deny_root" setting is not defined on both lines with the "pam_faillock.so" module, is commented out, or is missing from a line, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the operating system to automatically lock the root account, for a minimum of 15 minutes, when three unsuccessful logon attempts in 15 minutes are made.

Modify the first three lines of the auth section and the first line of the account section of the "/etc/pam.d/system-auth" and "/etc/pam.d/password-auth" files to match the following lines:

auth        required      pam_faillock.so preauth silent audit deny=3 even_deny_root fail_interval=900 unlock_time=900
auth        sufficient    pam_unix.so try_first_pass
auth        [default=die] pam_faillock.so authfail audit deny=3 even_deny_root fail_interval=900 unlock_time=900
account     required      pam_faillock.so

Note: Per requirement RHEL-07-010199, RHEL 7 must be configured to not overwrite custom authentication configuration settings while using the authconfig utility, otherwise manual changes to the listed files will be overwritten whenever the authconfig utility is used.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** By limiting the number of failed logon attempts, the risk of unauthorized system access via user password guessing, otherwise known as brute forcing, is reduced. Limits are imposed by locking the account.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000329-GPOS-00128, SRG-OS-000021-GPOS-00005

**Threat & control context:** Well-known accounts (root, Administrator, Guest) are guaranteed to exist with predictable names, which makes them ideal targets. Blocking direct logon forces attribution through named accounts (IA-2, AC-6(2)). Removing empty-password acceptance eliminates trivial access, and unique local admin passwords (LAPS) break pass-the-hash lateral movement across a fleet. Assess the effective result across every access path: console, SSH, RDP and network logon.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078.001 Valid Accounts: Default Accounts; T1078.003 Valid Accounts: Local Accounts; T1110 Brute Force

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002238**: Automatically lock the account or node for either an organization-defined time period, until the locked account or node is released by an administrator, or delays the next logon prompt according to the organization-defined delay algorithm when the maximum number of unsuccessful logon attempts is exceeded.  
  Rev 5: AC-7 b · Rev 4: AC-7 b · Rev 3: n/a

**Legacy IDs:** V-71945, SV-86569

### V-251703 · RHEL-07-010339 · CAT II: The Red Hat Enterprise Linux operating system must specify the default "include" directory for the /etc/sudoers file.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-251703r991589_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Privilege Elevation (UAC / sudo) |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must specify the default "include" directory for the /etc/sudoers file.

**Why it matters:** Even administrators work day-to-day without full power, and the system asks them to confirm, often by re-entering a password, before doing anything that could change important settings. That way, a harmful program can't quietly use admin power behind their back. It's like a bank requiring a second signature for large withdrawals.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *sudo*: A Linux command that lets an approved user temporarily act with administrator power.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sudo grep include /etc/sudoers
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sudo grep -r include /etc/sudoers.d
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** On RHEL, sudo policy lives in /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d/ (always edit with 'visudo', validate with 'visudo -c'). STIG items include removing NOPASSWD and !authenticate, setting 'Defaults timestamp_timeout=0', and restricting 'ALL ALL=(ALL) ALL'. 'su' is restricted to the wheel group with pam_wheel in /etc/pam.d/su.

**Operational impact:** Turning off password-less sudo affects automation such as Ansible and cron jobs. Use dedicated automation accounts with tightly scoped command lists and documented exceptions. Disabling UAC (EnableLUA = 0) is not acceptable and also breaks Store/UWP apps.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Note: If the "include" and "includedir" directives are not present in the /etc/sudoers file, this requirement is not applicable.

Verify the operating system specifies only the default "include" directory for the /etc/sudoers file with the following command:

$ sudo grep include /etc/sudoers

#includedir /etc/sudoers.d

If the results are not "/etc/sudoers.d" or additional files or directories are specified, this is a finding.

Verify the operating system does not have nested "include" files or directories within the /etc/sudoers.d directory with the following command:

$ sudo grep -r include /etc/sudoers.d

If results are returned, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the /etc/sudoers file to only include the /etc/sudoers.d directory.

Edit the /etc/sudoers file with the following command:

$ sudo visudo

Add or modify the following line:
#includedir /etc/sudoers.d
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The "sudo" command allows authorized users to run programs (including shells) as other users, system users, and root. The "/etc/sudoers" file is used to configure authorized "sudo" users as well as the programs they are allowed to run. Some configuration options in the "/etc/sudoers" file allow configured users to run programs without re-authenticating. Use of these configuration options makes it easier for one compromised account to be used to compromise other accounts.

It is possible to include other sudoers files from within the sudoers file currently being parsed using the #include and #includedir directives. When sudo reaches this line it will suspend processing of the current file (/etc/sudoers) and switch to the specified file/directory. Once the end of the included file(s) is reached, the rest of /etc/sudoers will be processed. Files that are included may themselves include other files. A hard limit of 128 nested include files is enforced to prevent include file loops.

**Threat & control context:** Elevation controls make privilege use deliberate, authenticated and auditable (AC-6(1)/(2)/(9)/(10), IA-11 re-authentication). UAC's secure-desktop prompt resists UI spoofing and input injection by malware running in the user's session. sudo restrictions (no NOPASSWD, no '!authenticate', short timestamp_timeout, no blanket ALL grants) prevent silent escalation by any process running as an admin user. Every elevation event should produce an audit record.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1548.002 Abuse Elevation Control: Bypass UAC; T1548.003 Abuse Elevation Control: Sudo and Sudo Caching; T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

**In plain terms:** This computer must restrict privilege elevation to authorized personnel.

**Why it matters:** Even administrators work day-to-day without full power, and the system asks them to confirm, often by re-entering a password, before doing anything that could change important settings. That way, a harmful program can't quietly use admin power behind their back. It's like a bank requiring a second signature for large withdrawals.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *sudo*: A Linux command that lets an approved user temporarily act with administrator power.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sudo grep -iw 'ALL' /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/*
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** On RHEL, sudo policy lives in /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d/ (always edit with 'visudo', validate with 'visudo -c'). STIG items include removing NOPASSWD and !authenticate, setting 'Defaults timestamp_timeout=0', and restricting 'ALL ALL=(ALL) ALL'. 'su' is restricted to the wheel group with pam_wheel in /etc/pam.d/su.

**Operational impact:** Turning off password-less sudo affects automation such as Ansible and cron jobs. Use dedicated automation accounts with tightly scoped command lists and documented exceptions. Disabling UAC (EnableLUA = 0) is not acceptable and also breaks Store/UWP apps.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the "sudoers" file restricts sudo access to authorized personnel.
$ sudo grep -iw 'ALL' /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/*

If the either of the following entries are returned, this is a finding:
ALL     ALL=(ALL) ALL
ALL     ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Remove the following entries from the sudoers file:
ALL     ALL=(ALL) ALL
ALL     ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The sudo command allows a user to execute programs with elevated (administrator) privileges. It prompts the user for their password and confirms your request to execute a command by checking a file, called sudoers. If the "sudoers" file is not configured correctly, any user defined on the system can initiate privileged actions on the target system.

**Threat & control context:** Elevation controls make privilege use deliberate, authenticated and auditable (AC-6(1)/(2)/(9)/(10), IA-11 re-authentication). UAC's secure-desktop prompt resists UI spoofing and input injection by malware running in the user's session. sudo restrictions (no NOPASSWD, no '!authenticate', short timestamp_timeout, no blanket ALL grants) prevent silent escalation by any process running as an admin user. Every elevation event should produce an audit record.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1548.002 Abuse Elevation Control: Bypass UAC; T1548.003 Abuse Elevation Control: Sudo and Sudo Caching; T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

```text
Verify that the sudoers security policy is configured to use the invoking user's password for privilege escalation.

```

#### Level 2: System Administrator

|---|---|---|---|

```text
If conflicting results are returned, this is a finding.
```

```text
Configure the "sudo" command to require re-authentication.
Edit the /etc/sudoers file:
$ sudo visudo

Add or modify the following line:
Defaults timestamp_timeout=[value]
Note: The "[value]" must be a number that is greater than or equal to "0".

Remove any duplicate or conflicting lines from /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d/ files.
```

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without re-authentication, users may access resources or perform tasks for which they do not have authorization.

When operating systems provide the capability to escalate a functional capability, it is critical the organization requires the user to re-authenticate when using the "sudo" command.

### V-255927 · RHEL-07-010375 · CAT III: The Red Hat Enterprise Linux operating system must restrict access to the kernel message buffer.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-255927r958524_rule` |
| Severity | CAT III (low) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000138-GPOS-00069 |
| Topic | Kernel & Memory Exploit Mitigations |
| CCI | CCI-001090 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-4 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-4 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-4 |
| Implemented via | Kernel parameter (sysctl) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must restrict access to the kernel message buffer.

**Why it matters:** Hackers often break in by tricking a program into running their own instructions. These settings turn on built-in defenses that shuffle where things sit in memory and refuse to run code from places it shouldn't come from. It's like a bank regularly moving the vault around and refusing to accept instructions written on deposit slips.

**How important is it?** Low priority (CAT III): This setting adds an extra layer of protection. A gap here on its own is less likely to cause harm, but it weakens the overall defenses.

**Key terms:**
- *Kernel parameter*: A low-level switch that changes how the core of the operating system behaves.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| sysctl | /etc/sysctl.d | kernel.dmesg_restrict | 1 |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sysctl kernel.dmesg_restrict
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep -r kernel.dmesg_restrict /run/sysctl.d/* /etc/sysctl.d/* /usr/local/lib/sysctl.d/* /usr/lib/sysctl.d/* /lib/sysctl.d/* /etc/sysctl.conf 2> /dev/null
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo grep -rs '^[[:space:]]*kernel.dmesg_restrict' /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/ /run/sysctl.d/ /usr/local/lib/sysctl.d/ /usr/lib/sysctl.d/ /lib/sysctl.d/
```

Expected: Every match must set 1. Conflicting values in other files are a finding.

**How it works:** On RHEL, kernel tunables are set in /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf (applied with 'sysctl --system' and verified with 'sysctl <key>'). Remember that a later file or /etc/sysctl.conf can override an earlier drop-in, and the STIG check typically greps all locations for conflicts. Boot parameters (e.g. 'vsyscall=none', 'page_poison=1', 'pti=on', 'slub_debug=P', 'audit=1') are set with 'grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args=...'. Core dumps are controlled through /etc/systemd/coredump.conf and 'ulimit -c'.

**Operational impact:** Restricting ptrace and dmesg affects debuggers (gdb, strace) for non-root users. Disabling core dumps removes crash diagnostics. HVCI can block older or unsigned drivers, so check driver compatibility first. Most sysctl changes are immediate, while boot parameters require a reboot.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the operating system is configured to restrict access to the kernel message buffer with the following commands:

     $ sudo sysctl kernel.dmesg_restrict
     kernel.dmesg_restrict = 1

If "kernel.dmesg_restrict" is not set to "1" or is missing, this is a finding.

Check that the configuration files are present to enable this kernel parameter:

     $ sudo grep -r kernel.dmesg_restrict /run/sysctl.d/* /etc/sysctl.d/* /usr/local/lib/sysctl.d/* /usr/lib/sysctl.d/* /lib/sysctl.d/* /etc/sysctl.conf 2> /dev/null
     /etc/sysctl.conf:kernel.dmesg_restrict = 1
     /etc/sysctl.d/99-sysctl.conf:kernel.dmesg_restrict = 1

If "kernel.dmesg_restrict" is not set to "1", is missing or commented out, this is a finding.

If conflicting results are returned, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the operating system to restrict access to the kernel message buffer.

Set the system to the required kernel parameter by adding or modifying the following line in /etc/sysctl.conf or a config file in the /etc/sysctl.d/ directory:

     kernel.dmesg_restrict = 1

Remove any configurations that conflict with the above from the following locations:
     /run/sysctl.d/
     /etc/sysctl.d/
     /usr/local/lib/sysctl.d/
     /usr/lib/sysctl.d/
     /lib/sysctl.d/
     /etc/sysctl.conf

Reload settings from all system configuration files with the following command:

     $ sudo sysctl --system
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Restricting access to the kernel message buffer limits access only to root. This prevents attackers from gaining additional system information as a non-privileged user.

**Threat & control context:** These mitigations don't remove vulnerabilities. They raise the cost and lower the reliability of exploiting them. ASLR, DEP/NX and SEHOP break classic memory-corruption techniques. Restricting ptrace, kernel pointer exposure, dmesg, unprivileged BPF and kexec removes common local-privilege-escalation primitives and information leaks. Hypervisor-enforced code integrity (HVCI) and VBS protect the kernel itself. These support SI-16 (memory protection), SC-39 (process isolation) and CM-6 baseline configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1055 Process Injection; T1014 Rootkit; T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution

**Severity rationale:** CAT III: any vulnerability whose existence degrades measures to protect against loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001090**: Prevent unauthorized and unintended information transfer via shared system resources.  
  Rev 5: SC-4 · Rev 4: SC-4 · Rev 3: SC-4
