| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules | -a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/su -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k privileged-priv_change |  |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sudo grep -w "/usr/bin/su" /etc/audit/audit.rules
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo auditctl -l | grep -- '/usr/bin/su'
```

Expected: Loaded rule matching: -a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/su -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k privileged-priv_change

**How it works:** On RHEL, sudo policy lives in /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d/ (always edit with 'visudo', validate with 'visudo -c'). STIG items include removing NOPASSWD and !authenticate, setting 'Defaults timestamp_timeout=0', and restricting 'ALL ALL=(ALL) ALL'. 'su' is restricted to the wheel group with pam_wheel in /etc/pam.d/su.

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** Turning off password-less sudo affects automation such as Ansible and cron jobs. Use dedicated automation accounts with tightly scoped command lists and documented exceptions. Disabling UAC (EnableLUA = 0) is not acceptable and also breaks Store/UWP apps.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the operating system generates audit records when successful/unsuccessful attempts to use the "su" command occur.

Check that the following system call is being audited by performing the following command to check the file system rules in "/etc/audit/audit.rules":

$ sudo grep -w "/usr/bin/su" /etc/audit/audit.rules

-a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/su -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k privileged-priv_change

If the command does not return any output, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the operating system to generate audit records when successful/unsuccessful attempts to use the "su" command occur.

Add or update the following rule in "/etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules":

-a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/su -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k privileged-priv_change

The audit daemon must be restarted for the changes to take effect.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Reconstruction of harmful events or forensic analysis is not possible if audit records do not contain enough information.

At a minimum, the organization must audit the full-text recording of privileged access commands. The organization must maintain audit trails in sufficient detail to reconstruct events to determine the cause and impact of compromise.

When a user logs on, the auid is set to the uid of the account that is being authenticated. Daemons are not user sessions and have the loginuid set to -1. The auid representation is an unsigned 32-bit integer, which equals 4294967295. The audit system interprets -1, 4294967295, and "unset" in the same way.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000037-GPOS-00015, SRG-OS-000042-GPOS-00020, SRG-OS-000392-GPOS-00172, SRG-OS-000462-GPOS-00206, SRG-OS-000471-GPOS-00215

**Threat & control context:** Elevation controls make privilege use deliberate, authenticated and auditable (AC-6(1)/(2)/(9)/(10), IA-11 re-authentication). UAC's secure-desktop prompt resists UI spoofing and input injection by malware running in the user's session. sudo restrictions (no NOPASSWD, no '!authenticate', short timestamp_timeout, no blanket ALL grants) prevent silent escalation by any process running as an admin user. Every elevation event should produce an audit record.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1548.002 Abuse Elevation Control: Bypass UAC; T1548.003 Abuse Elevation Control: Sudo and Sudo Caching; T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000130**: Ensure that audit records contain information that establishes what type of event occurred.  
  Rev 5: AU-3 a · Rev 4: AU-3 · Rev 3: AU-3
- **CCI-000135**: Generate audit records containing the organization-defined additional information that is to be included in the audit records.  
  Rev 5: AU-3 (1) · Rev 4: AU-3 (1) · Rev 3: AU-3 (1)
- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 c · Rev 4: AU-12 c · Rev 3: AU-12 c
- **CCI-002884**: Log organization-defined audit events for nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic sessions.  
  Rev 5: MA-4 (1) (a) · Rev 4: MA-4 (1) (a) · Rev 3: n/a

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules | -a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/chsh -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k privileged-priv_change |  |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sudo grep -w "/usr/bin/chsh" /etc/audit/audit.rules
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo auditctl -l | grep -- '/usr/bin/chsh'
```

Expected: Loaded rule matching: -a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/chsh -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k privileged-priv_change

**How it works:** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the operating system generates audit records when successful/unsuccessful attempts to use the "chsh" command occur.

Check that the following system call is being audited by performing the following command to check the file system rules in "/etc/audit/audit.rules":

$ sudo grep -w "/usr/bin/chsh" /etc/audit/audit.rules

-a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/chsh -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k privileged-priv_change

If the command does not return any output, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the operating system to generate audit records when successful/unsuccessful attempts to use the "chsh" command occur.

Add or update the following rule in "/etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules":

-a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/chsh -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k privileged-priv_change

The audit daemon must be restarted for the changes to take effect.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Reconstruction of harmful events or forensic analysis is not possible if audit records do not contain enough information.

At a minimum, the organization must audit the full-text recording of privileged access commands. The organization must maintain audit trails in sufficient detail to reconstruct events to determine the cause and impact of compromise.

When a user logs on, the auid is set to the uid of the account that is being authenticated. Daemons are not user sessions and have the loginuid set to -1. The auid representation is an unsigned 32-bit integer, which equals 4294967295. The audit system interprets -1, 4294967295, and "unset" in the same way.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000037-GPOS-00015, SRG-OS-000042-GPOS-00020, SRG-OS-000392-GPOS-00172, SRG-OS-000462-GPOS-00206, SRG-OS-000471-GPOS-00215

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000130**: Ensure that audit records contain information that establishes what type of event occurred.  
  Rev 5: AU-3 a · Rev 4: AU-3 · Rev 3: AU-3
- **CCI-000135**: Generate audit records containing the organization-defined additional information that is to be included in the audit records.  
  Rev 5: AU-3 (1) · Rev 4: AU-3 (1) · Rev 3: AU-3 (1)
- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 c · Rev 4: AU-12 c · Rev 3: AU-12 c
- **CCI-002884**: Log organization-defined audit events for nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic sessions.  
  Rev 5: MA-4 (1) (a) · Rev 4: MA-4 (1) (a) · Rev 3: n/a

**Legacy IDs:** SV-86791, V-72167

```text
sudo auditctl -l | grep -- '/usr/bin/mount'
```

**Also related (File System Layout & Mount Options):** On RHEL, partitions are defined at install time (/home, /tmp, /var, /var/log, /var/log/audit, /var/tmp). -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S mount -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k privileged-mount
```text
-a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/mount -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k privileged-mount

If all uses of the "mount" command are not being audited, this is a finding.
```

```text
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S mount -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k privileged-mount
-a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/mount -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k privileged-mount

The audit daemon must be restarted for the changes to take effect.
```

```text
Check that the following system call is being audited by performing the following command to check the file system rules in "/etc/audit/audit.rules":

$ sudo grep -w "/usr/sbin/postqueue" /etc/audit/audit.rules

-a always,exit -F path=/usr/sbin/postqueue -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k privileged-postfix

If the command does not return any output, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the operating system to generate audit records when successful/unsuccessful attempts to use the "postqueue" command occur.

Add or update the following rule in "/etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules":

-a always,exit -F path=/usr/sbin/postqueue -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k privileged-postfix

The audit daemon must be restarted for the changes to take effect.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Reconstruction of harmful events or forensic analysis is not possible if audit records do not contain enough information.

At a minimum, the organization must audit the full-text recording of privileged postfix commands. The organization must maintain audit trails in sufficient detail to reconstruct events to determine the cause and impact of compromise.

When a user logs on, the auid is set to the uid of the account that is being authenticated. Daemons are not user sessions and have the loginuid set to -1. The auid representation is an unsigned 32-bit integer, which equals 4294967295. The audit system interprets -1, 4294967295, and "unset" in the same way.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000042-GPOS-00020, SRG-OS-000392-GPOS-00172

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

| Implemented via | Audit rule |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must audit all uses of the ssh-keysign command.

**Why it matters:** SSH is the secure "remote control" administrators use to manage the computer over the network by typing commands. This rule tightens how that remote control works: who may use it, how they prove their identity, and how idle connections are closed. It's like making sure the building's service entrance has a good lock and isn't propped open.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules | -a always,exit -F path=/usr/libexec/openssh/ssh-keysign -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k privileged-ssh |  |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sudo grep -w "/usr/libexec/openssh/ssh-keysign" /etc/audit/audit.rules
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo auditctl -l | grep -- '/usr/libexec/openssh/ssh-keysign'
```

Expected: Loaded rule matching: -a always,exit -F path=/usr/libexec/openssh/ssh-keysign -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k privileged-ssh

**How it works:** sshd reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config, and on RHEL 9/10 also drop-ins under /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ that are processed in lexical order, where the first value obtained wins. Put STIG settings in an early-sorting drop-in (e.g. 00-stig.conf) so a vendor file can't silently override them. Validate syntax with 'sshd -t', check the effective configuration with 'sshd -T | grep -i <keyword>', then 'systemctl reload sshd'.

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** Keep an existing session open while you reload sshd so a typo can't lock you out. Disabling root login requires named admin accounts plus sudo. Idle timeouts (ClientAliveInterval/CountMax) will disconnect long-running interactive sessions, so use tmux or screen for those.

```text
-a always,exit -F path=/usr/libexec/openssh/ssh-keysign -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k privileged-ssh

If the command does not return any output, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text

The audit daemon must be restarted for the changes to take effect.
```

When a user logs on, the auid is set to the uid of the account that is being authenticated. Daemons are not user sessions and have the loginuid set to -1. The auid representation is an unsigned 32-bit integer, which equals 4294967295. The audit system interprets -1, 4294967295, and "unset" in the same way.

**Threat & control context:** SSH is the primary remote administration channel on Linux and therefore a high-value target. Hardening reduces the attack surface: no root or empty-password logins, no host-based trust (rhosts) or user environment injection, strict file-mode checks, idle-session termination, and approved cryptography only. These settings support AC-17 (Remote Access), AC-12, IA-2 and SC-8. Also check authorized_keys sprawl and key lifecycle, which no STIG setting fully covers.

### V-204560 · RHEL-07-030820 · CAT II: The Red Hat Enterprise Linux operating system must audit all uses of the init_module and finit_module syscalls.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-204560r991580_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000471-GPOS-00216 |
| Topic | Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-000172 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-12 c |
| Implemented via | Audit rule |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must audit all uses of the init_module and finit_module syscalls.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules | -a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S init_module,finit_module -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k modulechange |  |
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules | -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S init_module,finit_module -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k modulechange |  |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sudo grep init_module /etc/audit/audit.rules
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo auditctl -l | grep -- 'init_module'
```

Expected: Loaded rule matching: -a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S init_module,finit_module -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k modulechange

**How it works:** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the operating system generates audit records upon successful/unsuccessful attempts to use the "init_module" and "finit_module" syscalls.

Check the auditing rules in "/etc/audit/audit.rules" with the following command:

$ sudo grep init_module /etc/audit/audit.rules

-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S init_module,finit_module -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k modulechange

-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S init_module,finit_module -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k modulechange

If both the "b32" and "b64" audit rules are not defined for the "init_module" and "finit_module" syscalls, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the operating system to generate audit records upon successful/unsuccessful attempts to use the "init_module" and "finit_module" syscalls.

Add or update the following rules in "/etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules":

-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S init_module,finit_module -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k modulechange

-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S init_module,finit_module -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k modulechange

The audit daemon must be restarted for the changes to take effect.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without generating audit records that are specific to the security and mission needs of the organization, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate the events relating to an incident or identify those responsible for one.

Audit records can be generated from various components within the information system (e.g., module or policy filter).

The system call rules are loaded into a matching engine that intercepts each syscall made by all programs on the system. Therefore, it is very important to use syscall rules only when absolutely necessary since these affect performance. The more rules, the bigger the performance hit. The performance can be helped, however, by combining syscalls into one rule whenever possible.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000471-GPOS-00216, SRG-OS-000477-GPOS-00222

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 c · Rev 4: AU-12 c · Rev 3: AU-12 c

**Legacy IDs:** V-72187, SV-86811

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must generate audit records for all account creations, modifications, disabling, and termination events that affect /etc/gshadow.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |


Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text

```

Expected: Loaded rule matching: -w /etc/gshadow -p wa -k identity

**How it works:** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the operating system must generate audit records for all account creations, modifications, disabling, and termination events that affect "/etc/gshadow".

# grep /etc/gshadow /etc/audit/audit.rules

-w /etc/gshadow -p wa -k identity

If the command does not return a line, or the line is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the operating system to generate audit records for all account creations, modifications, disabling, and termination events that affect "/etc/gshadow".

Add or update the following rule in "/etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules":

-w /etc/gshadow -p wa -k identity

The audit daemon must be restarted for the changes to take effect.
```

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

### V-204572 · RHEL-07-030910 · CAT II: The Red Hat Enterprise Linux operating system must audit all uses of the unlink, unlinkat, rename, renameat, and rmdir syscalls.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-204572r991575_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000466-GPOS-00210 |
| Topic | Built-in & Privileged Account Hardening, Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-000172, CCI-002884 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-12 c, MA-4 (1) (a) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-12 c, MA-4 (1) (a) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-12 c |
| Implemented via | Audit rule |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must audit all uses of the unlink, unlinkat, rename, renameat, and rmdir syscalls.

**Why it matters:** Every computer comes with a few built-in "master" accounts whose names everyone knows. This rule makes those accounts harder to abuse, for example by not letting anyone log in directly as the master account and never allowing accounts with no password. It's like not leaving the master key labelled "MASTER KEY" hanging by the front door.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules | -a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S unlink,unlinkat,rename,renameat,rmdir -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k delete |  |
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules | -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S unlink,unlinkat,rename,renameat,rmdir -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k delete |  |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sudo grep 'unlink\|rename\|rmdir' /etc/audit/audit.rules
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo auditctl -l | grep -- 'unlink'
```

Expected: Loaded rule matching: -a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S unlink,unlinkat,rename,renameat,rmdir -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k delete

**How it works:** On RHEL, root logon is controlled through sshd ('PermitRootLogin no'), /etc/securetty (where present), and PAM. Empty passwords are blocked by removing 'nullok' from pam_unix in system-auth and password-auth and by setting 'PermitEmptyPasswords no' for sshd. Only root should have UID 0 ('awk -F: "$3==0" /etc/passwd').

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** Make sure at least one named administrator account with sudo or admin rights works before disabling root or Administrator logon paths. Renaming the built-in Administrator can break scripts that reference it by name.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the operating system generates audit records upon successful/unsuccessful attempts to use the "unlink", "unlinkat", "rename", "renameat", and "rmdir" syscalls.

Check the file system rules in "/etc/audit/audit.rules" with the following commands:

# grep 'unlink\|rename\|rmdir' /etc/audit/audit.rules

-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S unlink,unlinkat,rename,renameat,rmdir -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k delete

-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S unlink,unlinkat,rename,renameat,rmdir -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k delete

If both the "b32" and "b64" audit rules are not defined for the "unlink", "unlinkat", "rename", "renameat", and "rmdir" syscalls, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the operating system to generate audit records upon successful/unsuccessful attempts to use the "unlink", "unlinkat", "rename", "renameat", and "rmdir" syscalls.

Add the following rules in "/etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules":

-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S unlink,unlinkat,rename,renameat,rmdir -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k delete

-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S unlink,unlinkat,rename,renameat,rmdir -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k delete

The audit daemon must be restarted for the changes to take effect.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** If the system is not configured to audit certain activities and write them to an audit log, it is more difficult to detect and track system compromises and damages incurred during a system compromise.

When a user logs on, the auid is set to the uid of the account that is being authenticated. Daemons are not user sessions and have the loginuid set to -1. The auid representation is an unsigned 32-bit integer, which equals 4294967295. The audit system interprets -1, 4294967295, and "unset" in the same way.

The system call rules are loaded into a matching engine that intercepts each syscall made by all programs on the system. Therefore, it is very important to use syscall rules only when absolutely necessary since these affect performance. The more rules, the bigger the performance hit. The performance can be helped, however, by combining syscalls into one rule whenever possible.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000466-GPOS-00210, SRG-OS-000467-GPOS-00211, SRG-OS-000468-GPOS-00212, SRG-OS-000392-GPOS-00172

**Threat & control context:** Well-known accounts (root, Administrator, Guest) are guaranteed to exist with predictable names, which makes them ideal targets. Blocking direct logon forces attribution through named accounts (IA-2, AC-6(2)). Removing empty-password acceptance eliminates trivial access, and unique local admin passwords (LAPS) break pass-the-hash lateral movement across a fleet. Assess the effective result across every access path: console, SSH, RDP and network logon.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078.001 Valid Accounts: Default Accounts; T1078.003 Valid Accounts: Local Accounts; T1110 Brute Force; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 c · Rev 4: AU-12 c · Rev 3: AU-12 c
- **CCI-002884**: Log organization-defined audit events for nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic sessions.  
  Rev 5: MA-4 (1) (a) · Rev 4: MA-4 (1) (a) · Rev 3: n/a

**Legacy IDs:** V-72205, SV-86829

### V-204574 · RHEL-07-031000 · CAT II: The Red Hat Enterprise Linux operating system must send rsyslog output to a log aggregation server.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-204574r991589_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Audit Log Capacity, Offloading & Failure Handling |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must send rsyslog output to a log aggregation server.

**Why it matters:** The computer keeps a "security diary" of important events. This rule makes sure the diary has enough pages, that a copy is sent to a separate, safe location, and that someone is alerted if the diary fills up or stops working. It's like a store's security cameras recording to an off-site server so a thief can't simply take the tape.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep @ /etc/rsyslog.conf /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** On RHEL, auditd capacity and failure behavior are set in /etc/audit/auditd.conf (space_left, space_left_action, admin_space_left(_action), disk_full_action, disk_error_action, max_log_file(_action), action_mail_acct). Off-loading uses rsyslog (omfwd with TLS via gtls/ossl stream drivers) or the audisp-remote / audit 'remote' plugin. Put /var/log/audit on its own partition so it can't starve the root file system. Restart with 'service auditd restart', because systemctl is blocked for auditd.

**Operational impact:** Actions such as 'halt' or 'single' on disk-full prioritize integrity over availability and can take a production system down. Agree the action with the ISSO/AO and monitor free space proactively. Larger local logs consume disk; forwarding requires network connectivity and certificates for TLS.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify "rsyslog" is configured to send all messages to a log aggregation server.

Check the configuration of "rsyslog" with the following command:

Note: If another logging package is used, substitute the utility configuration file for "/etc/rsyslog.conf".

     # grep @ /etc/rsyslog.conf /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf

     *.* @@[logaggregationserver.example.mil]:[port]

If there are no lines in the "/etc/rsyslog.conf" or "/etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf" files that contain the "@" or "@@" symbol(s), and the lines with the correct symbol(s) to send output to another system do not cover all "rsyslog" output, ask the system administrator to indicate how the audit logs are offloaded to a different system or media.

If the lines are commented out or there is no evidence that the audit logs are being sent to another log aggregation server, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Modify the "/etc/rsyslog.conf" or an "/etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf" file to contain a configuration line to send all "rsyslog" output to a log aggregation server:

For UDP:
     *.* @[logaggregationserver.example.mil]:[port]

For TCP:
     *.* @@[logaggregationserver.example.mil]:[port]
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Sending rsyslog output to another system ensures that the logs cannot be removed or modified in the event that the system is compromised or has a hardware failure.

**Threat & control context:** Logs that roll over, fill the disk or exist only on the compromised host can't support incident response. Attackers routinely clear or flood local logs. AU-4 (storage capacity), AU-4(1) (transfer to alternate storage), AU-5 (response to processing failures) and AU-9(2) (backup onto a separate system) require sized local storage, real-time off-host forwarding, and defined behavior (alert, halt or single-user) when audit capability is lost. Validate end-to-end delivery at the SIEM, not just the client configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070 Indicator Removal; T1562.006 Impair Defenses: Indicator Blocking

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

**Legacy IDs:** SV-86833, V-72209

### V-204575 · RHEL-07-031010 · CAT II: The Red Hat Enterprise Linux operating system must be configured so that the rsyslog daemon does not accept log messages from other servers unless the server is being used for log aggregation.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-204575r991589_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Audit Log Capacity, Offloading & Failure Handling, System Services & Daemons |
| CCI | CCI-000318, CCI-000368, CCI-001812, CCI-001813, CCI-001814 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-3 f, CM-6 c, CM-5 (1) (a) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-3 f, CM-6 c, CM-11 (2), CM-5 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-3 e, CM-6 c |
| Implemented via | Procedural / documentation |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured so that the rsyslog daemon does not accept log messages from other servers unless the server is being used for log aggregation.

**Why it matters:** The computer keeps a "security diary" of important events. This rule makes sure the diary has enough pages, that a copy is sent to a separate, safe location, and that someone is alerted if the diary fills up or stops working. It's like a store's security cameras recording to an off-site server so a thief can't simply take the tape.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Procedural / documentation. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep imtcp /etc/rsyslog.conf
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep imudp /etc/rsyslog.conf
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep imrelp /etc/rsyslog.conf
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** On RHEL, auditd capacity and failure behavior are set in /etc/audit/auditd.conf (space_left, space_left_action, admin_space_left(_action), disk_full_action, disk_error_action, max_log_file(_action), action_mail_acct). Off-loading uses rsyslog (omfwd with TLS via gtls/ossl stream drivers) or the audisp-remote / audit 'remote' plugin. Put /var/log/audit on its own partition so it can't starve the root file system. Restart with 'service auditd restart', because systemctl is blocked for auditd.

**Also related (System Services & Daemons):** On RHEL, use 'systemctl enable --now <unit>' for required services and 'systemctl disable --now <unit>' plus 'systemctl mask <unit>' for prohibited ones. Masking prevents a service from being started manually or as a dependency. Check with 'systemctl is-enabled <unit>' and 'systemctl is-active <unit>', and remember the matching .socket units.

**Operational impact:** Actions such as 'halt' or 'single' on disk-full prioritize integrity over availability and can take a production system down. Agree the action with the ISSO/AO and monitor free space proactively. Larger local logs consume disk; forwarding requires network connectivity and certificates for TLS.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify that the system is not accepting "rsyslog" messages from other systems unless it is documented as a log aggregation server.

Check the configuration of "rsyslog" with the following command:

# grep imtcp /etc/rsyslog.conf
$ModLoad imtcp
# grep imudp /etc/rsyslog.conf
$ModLoad imudp
# grep imrelp /etc/rsyslog.conf
$ModLoad imrelp

If any of the above modules are being loaded in the "/etc/rsyslog.conf" file, ask to see the documentation for the system being used for log aggregation.

If the documentation does not exist, or does not specify the server as a log aggregation system, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Modify the "/etc/rsyslog.conf" file to remove the "ModLoad imtcp", "ModLoad imudp", and "ModLoad imrelp" configuration lines, or document the system as being used for log aggregation.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Unintentionally running a rsyslog server accepting remote messages puts the system at increased risk. Malicious rsyslog messages sent to the server could exploit vulnerabilities in the server software itself, could introduce misleading information in to the system's logs, or could fill the system's storage leading to a Denial of Service.

If the system is intended to be a log aggregation server its use must be documented with the ISSO.

**Threat & control context:** Logs that roll over, fill the disk or exist only on the compromised host can't support incident response. Attackers routinely clear or flood local logs. AU-4 (storage capacity), AU-4(1) (transfer to alternate storage), AU-5 (response to processing failures) and AU-9(2) (backup onto a separate system) require sized local storage, real-time off-host forwarding, and defined behavior (alert, halt or single-user) when audit capability is lost. Validate end-to-end delivery at the SIEM, not just the client configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070 Indicator Removal; T1562.006 Impair Defenses: Indicator Blocking; T1543 Create or Modify System Process; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000318**: Monitor and review activities associated with configuration-controlled changes to the system.  
  Rev 5: CM-3 f · Rev 4: CM-3 f · Rev 3: CM-3 e
- **CCI-000368**: Document any deviations from the established configuration settings for organization-defined system components based on organization-defined operational requirements.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 c · Rev 4: CM-6 c · Rev 3: CM-6 c
- **CCI-001812**: The information system prohibits user installation of software without explicit privileged status.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: CM-11 (2) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-001813**: Enforce access restrictions using organization-defined mechanisms.  
  Rev 5: CM-5 (1) (a) · Rev 4: CM-5 (1) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-001814**: The Information system supports auditing of the enforcement actions.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: CM-5 (1) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-214801 · RHEL-07-032000 · CAT I: The Red Hat Enterprise Linux operating system must use a virus scan program.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-214801r991589_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Anti-Malware & Reputation Protection |
| CCI | CCI-001668, CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SI-3 a, CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must use a virus scan program.

**Why it matters:** This keeps the computer's virus scanner switched on and up to date, and warns people before they open files or websites known to be dangerous. It's the digital equivalent of a smoke detector with fresh batteries.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

No single command can validate this rule. It is a procedural or manual check; follow the DISA check procedure.

**How it works:** On RHEL, use the enterprise-approved endpoint product (e.g. Trellix/ENSL). Verify that the agent service is active and its definitions are current.

**Operational impact:** Real-time scanning adds I/O overhead. Define vetted exclusions for databases and build directories only with ISSO approval and document them.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify an anti-virus solution is installed on the system. The anti-virus solution may be bundled with an approved host-based security solution.

If there is no anti-virus solution installed on the system, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Install an antivirus solution on the system.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Virus scanning software can be used to protect a system from penetration from computer viruses and to limit their spread through intermediate systems.

The virus scanning software should be configured to perform scans dynamically on accessed files. If this capability is not available, the system must be configured to scan, at a minimum, all altered files on the system on a daily basis.

If the system processes inbound SMTP mail, the virus scanner must be configured to scan all received mail.

**Threat & control context:** Signature and behavioral anti-malware, together with reputation services such as SmartScreen, address commodity and opportunistic threats at the endpoint (SI-3 malicious code protection, SI-3(2) automatic updates). DoD typically requires an approved enterprise endpoint-security suite. The STIG check confirms that a capable product is installed, running and updating, and that users can't bypass warnings.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.001 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools; T1204 User Execution; T1566 Phishing

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001668**: The organization employs malicious code protection mechanisms at workstations, servers, or mobile computing devices on the network to detect and eradicate malicious code transported by electronic mail, electronic mail attachments, web accesses, removable media, or other common means or inserted through the exploitation of information system vulnerabilities.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: SI-3 a
- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-204576 · RHEL-07-040000 · CAT III: The Red Hat Enterprise Linux operating system must limit the number of concurrent sessions to 10 for all accounts and/or account types.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-204576r958398_rule` |
| Severity | CAT III (low) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000027-GPOS-00008 |
| Topic | Authentication Stack (PAM, SSSD, Directory) |
| CCI | CCI-000054 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-10 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-10 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-10 |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must limit the number of concurrent sessions to 10 for all accounts and/or account types.

**Why it matters:** Behind the sign-in screen is a chain of checks: the password is right, the account isn't locked, the password isn't expired, and so on. This rule makes sure every check in that chain is present and in the correct order, like making sure every guard at a multi-checkpoint entrance is at their post.

**How important is it?** Low priority (CAT III): This setting adds an extra layer of protection. A gap here on its own is less likely to cause harm, but it weakens the overall defenses.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sudo grep "maxlogins" /etc/security/limits.conf /etc/security/limits.d/*.conf
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** On RHEL, PAM stacks live in /etc/pam.d/ (system-auth, password-auth, login, sshd, su). Manage them through authselect profiles ('authselect select sssd with-faillock with-mkhomedir ...', 'authselect current'), because authselect overwrites hand edits. Custom changes belong in a custom profile ('authselect create-profile'). SSSD is configured in /etc/sssd/sssd.conf and conf.d/ (mode 0600, owned by root), and you restart sssd after changes. Concurrent session limits are set in /etc/security/limits.conf ('* hard maxlogins 10').

**Operational impact:** PAM mistakes can lock everyone out, including root. Test changes from a second, still-open root session, and keep console access available.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the operating system limits the number of concurrent sessions to "10" for all accounts and/or account types by issuing the following command:

# grep "maxlogins" /etc/security/limits.conf /etc/security/limits.d/*.conf

* hard maxlogins 10

This can be set as a global domain (with the * wildcard) but may be set differently for multiple domains.

If the "maxlogins" item is missing, commented out, or the value is not set to "10" or less for all domains that have the "maxlogins" item assigned, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the operating system to limit the number of concurrent sessions to "10" for all accounts and/or account types.

Add the following line to the top of the /etc/security/limits.conf or in a ".conf" file defined in /etc/security/limits.d/ :

* hard maxlogins 10
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Operating system management includes the ability to control the number of users and user sessions that utilize an operating system. Limiting the number of allowed users and sessions per user is helpful in reducing the risks related to DoS attacks.

This requirement addresses concurrent sessions for information system accounts and does not address concurrent sessions by single users via multiple system accounts. The maximum number of concurrent sessions should be defined based on mission needs and the operational environment for each system.

**Threat & control context:** PAM and SSSD define how every Linux authentication decision is made. Misordered or optional modules silently bypass controls such as faillock, pwquality and pwhistory. Credential caching lifetimes trade availability against revocation latency, so a revoked account keeps working offline until its cache expires. These settings support IA-2, IA-5(13) (expiration of cached authenticators), AC-7, AC-9 (previous logon notification) and AC-10 (concurrent session control).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1556.003 Modify Authentication Process: Pluggable Authentication Modules; T1110 Brute Force

**Severity rationale:** CAT III: any vulnerability whose existence degrades measures to protect against loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000054**: Limit the number of concurrent sessions for each organization-defined account and/or account type to an organization-defined number.  
  Rev 5: AC-10 · Rev 4: AC-10 · Rev 3: AC-10

**Legacy IDs:** V-72217, SV-86841

### V-204577 · RHEL-07-040100 · CAT II: The Red Hat Enterprise Linux operating system must be configured to prohibit or restrict the use of functions, ports, protocols, and/or services, as defined in the Ports, Protocols, and Services Management Component Local Service Assessment (PPSM CLSA) and vulnerability assessments.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-204577r958480_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000096-GPOS-00050 |
| Topic | Host Firewall, System Services & Daemons |
| CCI | CCI-000382, CCI-002314 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 b, AC-17 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 b, AC-17 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured to prohibit or restrict the use of functions, ports, protocols, and/or services, as defined in the Ports, Protocols, and Services Management Component Local Service Assessment (PPSM CLSA) and vulnerability assessments.

**Why it matters:** A firewall is a gatekeeper that decides which network connections are allowed in and out of the computer. This rule makes sure the gatekeeper is switched on and turns away anything that isn't on the approved list, like a security guard who only lets in people with an appointment.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Firewall*: A filter that decides which network connections are allowed in or out.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
firewall-cmd --list-all
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** On RHEL, use firewalld (systemctl enable --now firewalld) with nftables as the backend (FirewallBackend=nftables in /etc/firewalld/firewalld.conf). Set the default zone to drop or deny and add only the required services and ports ('firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=...', then '--reload'). Review with 'firewall-cmd --list-all-zones'.

**Also related (System Services & Daemons):** On RHEL, use 'systemctl enable --now <unit>' for required services and 'systemctl disable --now <unit>' plus 'systemctl mask <unit>' for prohibited ones. Masking prevents a service from being started manually or as a dependency. Check with 'systemctl is-enabled <unit>' and 'systemctl is-active <unit>', and remember the matching .socket units.

**Operational impact:** An over-restrictive default can cut off management or application traffic. Make changes from the console, or stage them with a timed rollback ('firewall-cmd --timeout').

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Inspect the firewall configuration and running services to verify that it is configured to prohibit or restrict the use of functions, ports, protocols, and/or services that are unnecessary or prohibited.

Check which services are currently active with the following command:

# firewall-cmd --list-all
public (default, active)
  interfaces: enp0s3
  sources:
  services: dhcpv6-client dns http https ldaps rpc-bind ssh
  ports:
  masquerade: no
  forward-ports:
  icmp-blocks:
  rich rules:

Ask the System Administrator for the site or program PPSM CLSA. Verify the services allowed by the firewall match the PPSM CLSA.

If there are additional ports, protocols, or services that are not in the PPSM CLSA, or there are ports, protocols, or services that are prohibited by the PPSM Category Assurance List (CAL), this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Update the host's firewall settings and/or running services to comply with the PPSM CLSA for the site or program and the PPSM CAL.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** In order to prevent unauthorized connection of devices, unauthorized transfer of information, or unauthorized tunneling (i.e., embedding of data types within data types), organizations must disable or restrict unused or unnecessary physical and logical ports/protocols on information systems.

Operating systems are capable of providing a wide variety of functions and services. Some of the functions and services provided by default may not be necessary to support essential organizational operations. Additionally, it is sometimes convenient to provide multiple services from a single component (e.g., VPN and IPS); however, doing so increases risk over limiting the services provided by any one component.

To support the requirements and principles of least functionality, the operating system must support the organizational requirements, providing only essential capabilities and limiting the use of ports, protocols, and/or services to only those required, authorized, and approved to conduct official business or to address authorized quality of life issues.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000096-GPOS-00050, SRG-OS-000297-GPOS-00115

**Threat & control context:** A host firewall enforces deny-by-default, allow-by-exception at the endpoint (SC-7(5)) and contains lateral movement even when the perimeter is breached or the host sits on a flat network. Exposed ports must match the system's PPSM registration (CM-7(1)). Remote-management exceptions should be scoped to authorized management hosts rather than 'any'. Check that the firewall service can't be stopped by non-administrators and that rule changes are audited.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.004 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify System Firewall; T1021 Remote Services; T1046 Network Service Discovery; T1543 Create or Modify System Process; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000382**: Configure the system to prohibit or restrict the use of organization-defined prohibited or restricted functions, system ports, protocols, software, and/or services.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 b · Rev 4: CM-7 b · Rev 3: CM-7
- **CCI-002314**: Employ automated mechanisms to control remote access methods.  
  Rev 5: AC-17 (1) · Rev 4: AC-17 (1) · Rev 3: n/a

**Legacy IDs:** V-72219, SV-86843

### V-204578 · RHEL-07-040110 · CAT II: The Red Hat Enterprise Linux 7 operating system must implement DoD-approved encryption to protect the confidentiality of SSH connections.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-204578r958408_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000033-GPOS-00014 |
| Topic | Approved Cryptography (FIPS 140), SSH Remote Administration |
| CCI | CCI-000068, CCI-000366, CCI-000803 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-17 (2), CM-6 b, IA-7 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-17 (2), CM-6 b, IA-7 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-17 (2), CM-6 b, IA-7 |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must implement DoD-approved encryption to protect the confidentiality of SSH connections.

**Why it matters:** Encryption is how computers scramble information so eavesdroppers can't read it. Some older scrambling methods have been "cracked" and are no longer safe. This rule makes the computer use only methods the U.S. government has tested and approved, like requiring modern, certified locks instead of old ones that a locksmith can easily pick.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *SSH*: Secure Shell: an encrypted way to control a computer remotely by typing commands.
- *FIPS 140*: A U.S. government standard for testing and approving encryption software.
- *DoD / DoW*: Department of Defense (renamed Department of War in recent DISA publications).

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/ssh/sshd_config | Ciphers | aes256-ctr,aes192-ctr,aes128-ctr |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sudo grep -i ciphers /etc/ssh/sshd_config
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo sshd -T | grep -i '^Ciphers '
```

Expected: ciphers aes256-ctr,aes192-ctr,aes128-ctr (the effective value sshd is using).

**How it works:** RHEL centralizes crypto settings in system-wide crypto policies: 'fips-mode-setup --enable' (RHEL 8) or 'fips=1' on the kernel command line at install time (RHEL 9/10), then 'update-crypto-policies --set FIPS'. Back-end files under /etc/crypto-policies/back-ends/ (openssh, opensslcnf, bind, gnutls and others) are generated from the policy, and individual services such as sshd must be pointed at them rather than hard-coding algorithms. Verify with 'fips-mode-setup --check' and 'update-crypto-policies --show'.

**Also related (SSH Remote Administration):** sshd reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config, and on RHEL 9/10 also drop-ins under /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ that are processed in lexical order, where the first value obtained wins. Put STIG settings in an early-sorting drop-in (e.g. 00-stig.conf) so a vendor file can't silently override them. Validate syntax with 'sshd -t', check the effective configuration with 'sshd -T | grep -i <keyword>', then 'systemctl reload sshd'.

**Operational impact:** Enabling FIPS mode can break applications that use non-approved algorithms (MD5 for non-security checksums, older Java code, legacy VPN or SSH clients). Enable it at install time where possible, because switching an existing RHEL 9/10 system into FIPS mode is not supported for production. Test interoperating systems before rollout.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the operating system uses mechanisms meeting the requirements of applicable federal laws, Executive orders, directives, policies, regulations, standards, and guidance for authentication to a cryptographic module.

The location of the "sshd_config" file may vary if a different daemon is in use.

Inspect the "Ciphers" configuration with the following command:

# grep -i ciphers /etc/ssh/sshd_config
Ciphers aes256-ctr,aes192-ctr,aes128-ctr

If any ciphers other than "aes256-ctr", "aes192-ctr", or "aes128-ctr" are listed, the order differs from the example above, the "Ciphers" keyword is missing, or the returned line is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure SSH to use FIPS 140-2 approved cryptographic algorithms.

Add the following line (or modify the line to have the required value) to the "/etc/ssh/sshd_config" file (this file may be named differently or be in a different location if using a version of SSH that is provided by a third-party vendor).

Ciphers aes256-ctr,aes192-ctr,aes128-ctr

The SSH service must be restarted for changes to take effect.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Unapproved mechanisms that are used for authentication to the cryptographic module are not verified and therefore cannot be relied upon to provide confidentiality or integrity, and DoD data may be compromised.

Operating systems utilizing encryption are required to use FIPS-compliant mechanisms for authenticating to cryptographic modules.

FIPS 140-2 is the current standard for validating that mechanisms used to access cryptographic modules utilize authentication that meets DoD requirements. This allows for Security Levels 1, 2, 3, or 4 for use on a general purpose computing system.

The system will attempt to use the first cipher presented by the client that matches the server list. Listing the values "strongest to weakest" is a method to ensure the use of the strongest cipher available to secure the SSH connection.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000033-GPOS-00014, SRG-OS-000120-GPOS-00061, SRG-OS-000125-GPOS-00065, SRG-OS-000250-GPOS-00093, SRG-OS-000393-GPOS-00173

**Threat & control context:** Federal systems must use FIPS 140-validated cryptographic modules (SC-13). Weak or legacy algorithms (MD5, SHA-1 MACs, CBC-mode ciphers, RC4, DES/3DES, small DH groups) enable downgrade, decryption or forgery attacks against data in transit (SC-8, SC-8(1)). The control is only as strong as its weakest negotiated option, so assessors look at the full allowed list, not just the preferred algorithm. Note that FIPS mode validates the module, not the protocol configuration, so both must be checked.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1040 Network Sniffing; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1600 Weaken Encryption; T1021.004 Remote Services: SSH; T1110 Brute Force; T1098.004 Account Manipulation: SSH Authorized Keys

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000068**: Implement cryptographic mechanisms to protect the confidentiality of remote access sessions.

### V-204579 · RHEL-07-040160 · CAT II: The Red Hat Enterprise Linux operating system must be configured so that all network connections associated with a communication session are terminated at the end of the session or after 15 minutes of inactivity from the user at a command prompt, except to fulfill documented and validated mission requirements.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-204579r970703_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000163-GPOS-00072 |
| Topic | Session Lock & Inactivity Timeout |
| CCI | CCI-001133, CCI-002361 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-10, AC-12 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-10, AC-12 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-10 |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured so that all network connections associated with a communication session are terminated at the end of the session or after 15 minutes of inactivity from the user at a command prompt, except to fulfill documented and validated mission requirements.

**Why it matters:** If you walk away from the computer and forget to lock it, it will lock itself after a short time (15 minutes for DoD) and hide what was on the screen. Anyone who sits down then has to sign in again. It's like a car that locks its doors automatically when you walk away.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/profile.d/tmout.sh | declare | -xr TMOUT=900 |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep -irw tmout /etc/profile /etc/bashrc /etc/profile.d
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo grep -si '^[[:space:]]*declare\b' /etc/profile.d/tmout.sh
```

Expected: declare -xr TMOUT=900

**How it works:** On RHEL, set GNOME locking through dconf in /etc/dconf/db/local.d/ (org/gnome/desktop/session idle-delay=uint32 900, org/gnome/desktop/screensaver lock-enabled=true, lock-delay=uint32 5) and lock each key in /etc/dconf/db/local.d/locks/ so users can't override it. Then run 'dconf update'. For terminals, set TMOUT=900 (readonly) in /etc/profile.d/. Network and SSH sessions use ClientAliveInterval/CountMax and systemd-logind StopIdleSessionSec.

**Operational impact:** Users running long unattended interactive jobs may be disconnected. Kiosk or operations displays that must stay visible need a documented exception and compensating physical controls.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the operating system terminates all network connections associated with a communications session at the end of the session or based on inactivity.

Check the value of the system inactivity timeout with the following command:

$ sudo grep -irw tmout /etc/profile /etc/bashrc /etc/profile.d

etc/profile.d/tmout.sh:declare -xr TMOUT=900

If conflicting results are returned, this is a finding.
If "TMOUT" is not set to "900" or less to enforce session termination after inactivity, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the operating system to terminate all network connections associated with a communications session at the end of the session or after a period of inactivity.

Create a script to enforce the inactivity timeout (for example /etc/profile.d/tmout.sh) such as:

#!/bin/bash

declare -xr TMOUT=900
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Terminating an idle session within a short time period reduces the window of opportunity for unauthorized personnel to take control of a management session enabled on the console or console port that has been left unattended. In addition, quickly terminating an idle session will also free up resources committed by the managed network element.

Terminating network connections associated with communications sessions includes, for example, de-allocating associated TCP/IP address/port pairs at the operating system level and de-allocating networking assignments at the application level if multiple application sessions are using a single operating system-level network connection. This does not mean that the operating system terminates all sessions or network access; it only ends the inactive session and releases the resources associated with that session.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000029-GPOS-00010, SRG-OS-000163-GPOS-00072

**Threat & control context:** Unattended, unlocked sessions are an opportunistic access path for insiders and visitors, so physical access becomes logical access. AC-11 (device lock, 15 minutes in DoD), AC-11(1) (pattern-hiding displays) and AC-12 (session termination) require automatic locking that the user can't override, re-authentication to unlock, and concealment of on-screen content. Smart-card removal locking extends this to CAC workflows.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001133**: Terminate the network connection associated with a communications session at the end of the session or after an organization-defined time period of inactivity.  
  Rev 5: SC-10 · Rev 4: SC-10 · Rev 3: SC-10
- **CCI-002361**: Automatically terminate a user session after organization-defined conditions or trigger events requiring session disconnect.  
  Rev 5: AC-12 · Rev 4: AC-12 · Rev 3: n/a

**Legacy IDs:** SV-86847, V-72223
